Announcing New vLLM and SGLang Inference Engines on TPU - Google Developers Blog 

# Announcing New vLLM and SGLang Inference Engines on TPU

OCT. 20, 2026

 Qi Zhou Principal Software Engineer 

 Chris Chan Group Product Manager 

As part of our broader announcements for PyTorch today, we are excited to launch native PyTorch backends for vLLM (developed in partnership with Inferact) and SGLang (developed in partnership with RadixArk).

## Background

For years, TPUs have powered large-scale AI workloads with high performance and efficiency. With the rise of agentic and multimodal workloads, serving efficiently is more important than ever. Both engines already run on TPU through JAX-based backends, but we kept hearing from developers that they wanted to customize and debug their serving stack in PyTorch.

So we started in earnest on TorchTPU, which runs PyTorch natively on TPU. We then built new vLLM and SGLang engines on top of it.

Our goal is for the PyTorch community to bring models to TPU and make them fast using the tools developers are already familiar with. The engines come with optimized, production-ready serving features and custom Pallas kernels.

...

## Workload support

Both engines are built for the full range of production workloads.

Here’s the list of supported features:

- Agentic & Multi-Turn: Automatic prefix caching, including for hybrid models; KV cache offloading to host memory and Managed Lustre through TPU Sync; tool calling and structured output
- Interactive & Low Latency: Speculative decoding with MTP, EAGLE-3, DFlash, DSpark and n-gram drafters
- High-throughput Batch: Data-parallel attention with expert parallelism
- Long Context: Context parallelism for prefill and decode; FP8 KV cache; host KV offloading
- Disaggregated Serving: Prefill and decode on separate hosts over TPU Sync, including between different parallel layouts
- Multimodal: Vision-language models with image and video input; embedding models
- Very Large Models: Hybrid and sparse-attention architectures, tensor, data, expert, pipeline and context parallelism across hosts; FP8, FP4 (MXFP4, NVFP4), INT8 and INT4 checkpoints

...

## Running today in production & public benchmarks

Both engines are already running at scale in production with preview customers. To provide transparent, reproducible proof of our performance, we benchmark in public through the community-standard SemiAnalysis InferenceX project.

Building on our initial submission of Qwen 3.5 on Ironwood TPU (TPU 7x), our engineering teams have further optimized the stack, bringing the lowest cost per million tokens overall to an industry leading 2.01 cents. Alongside these improvements, we have also published new state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance results to AgentX, the project's dedicated track for evaluating agentic long-context and multi-turn workloads. Ironwood TPU leads across most of the Pareto frontier. We look forward to continuously updating our public performance profiles as we bring more models and configurations to the leaderboard.

signals.title: Announcing Humming: Fast, Flexible Kernels for Quantized Inference | vLLM Blog
signals.excerpt:
Announcing Humming: Fast, Flexible Kernels for Quantized Inference | vLLM Blog

# Announcing Humming: Fast, Flexible Kernels for Quantized Inference

October 21, 2026 19 min read

Table of Contents

Ant Group and the vLLM community are open-sourcing Humming, a general-purpose, high-performance kernel library for quantized inference. Humming offers the following features:

- Broad device support: Supports NVIDIA GPU architectures from Turing onward, along with CUDA-compatible devices such as T-Head's Zhenwu 810E.
- Extensive quantization support: A unified architecture supports diverse combinations of weight and activation formats for dense and MoE workloads, covering a wide range of integer and floating-point types, bit widths, and scaling schemes.
- Strong execution performance: Significantly outperforms existing implementations from vLLM Marlin, FlashInfer, and DeepGEMM across many representative workloads.

Repository: github.com/vllm-project/humming

...

As models and inference workloads grow, memory capacity, memory bandwidth, and compute costs increasingly constrain deployment. This is especially apparent in MoE models: each token activates only a subset of experts, but the full set of weights still needs to be stored. DeepSeek-V3, for example, has 671 billion parameters, with 37 billion activated per token. Quantization lowers the precision of weights and activations to reduce memory usage and data movement, and can also improve compute efficiency.

Quantization requirements vary across models and GPU generations. Common configurations include WNA16, W8A8, W4A8, and W4A4, where W and A specify weight and activation bit widths, and N denotes a variable weight bit width. Even at the same precision, schemes such as INT4 and NVFP4 differ in numeric format and scaling. Scaling granularity, scale representation, group size, and symmetric or asymmetric quantization further expand the configuration space.

These storage and compute savings only translate into lower latency and higher throughput with efficient kernels. Prefill, decode, and varying MoE expert loads place different demands on compute and memory. Kernels must adapt to these workloads while keeping conversion, dequantization, and scheduling overhead low.

...

## General-Purpose Architecture

Humming's execution path has three parts: represent the quantized computation, select configurations for the hardware and workload, and compile a kernel from CUDA components.

...

### Broad Device Support

Humming's unified architecture enables broad GPU support. For NVIDIA GPUs, Humming fully supports every architecture from Turing onward, bringing a common quantized computing framework to multiple generations of hardware.

The unified JIT architecture also makes it straightforward to extend Humming to other GPUs compatible with CUDA programming. Humming already fully supports T-Head's Zhenwu 810E, bringing its shared kernels and tuning capabilities to more hardware platforms.

...

#### End-to-End Inference Performance

Humming's W4A8 gains extend to model serving. In our DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash test on eight H20 GPUs with TP=8, keeping the model's MXFP4 weights unchanged and switching MoE execution from Marlin W4A16 (BF16 activations) to Humming W4A8 (tokenwise FP8 activations) improves end-to-end throughput by approximately 14%–43% and reduces mean time to first token (TTFT) by approximately 25%–32%. The throughput advantage grows with concurrency: at concurrency 64, output throughput rises from 442.37 to 633.94 tokens/s, while mean time per output token (TPOT) falls by approximately 31%.

signals.title: Running Frontier-Class AI Models Across 8 NVIDIA DGX Spark Nodes | NVIDIA Technical Blog
signals.excerpt:
# Running Frontier-Class AI Models Across 8 NVIDIA DGX Spark Nodes

 Oct 22, 2026 

 By Arvind Gopalakrishnan, Eugene Rakhmatulin, Manini Sharma and Prerit Rodney 

 AI-Generated Summary 

- NVIDIA DGX Spark now supports official eight-node clusters, scaling unified memory to 1 TB and enabling local execution of frontier-class models such as the full GLM 5.3 (753B) from Z.ai.
- A Spark-optimized collective backend called RoCEnante reduces all-reduce latency for tensor-parallel decode on switch-connected clusters, delivering a 4.43x decode speedup at eight nodes compared to 3.05x without it.
- Benchmark data shows decode throughput scaling from roughly 12 tokens per second on one node to 52 tokens per second on eight nodes using Qwen3.8-27B (NVFP4), with switch topologies enabling flexible workload partitioning and ring topologies offering cost-effective four-node inference.
- NVIDIA NeMo Switchyard routes requests between model pools on a shared eight-node cluster, matching Qwen-only quality on a tool-use benchmark while raising aggregate throughput up to 3x when most traffic shifts to a smaller model.
- Pre-training a nanochat model from scratch across eight nodes achieves a 7.79x speedup at 97.4% scaling efficiency, demonstrating near-linear training performance for small models on the desk.

...

AI developers aren’t just running a single model anymore—they’re orchestrating multiple models in parallel, chaining inference calls, and experimenting with frontier-class architectures that demand hundreds of gigabytes of memory. NVIDIA DGX Spark was built to bring AI development to the desk, and now you’ll be able to link even more Spark nodes together. 

At GTC Berlin, NVIDIA announced official support for eight-node DGX Spark clusters, scaling unified memory to 1 TB and opening the door to frontier-class models, multi-agent workloads, and near-linear pre-training—all running locally.

NVIDIA Sync makes it easy to cluster. Its Cluster Assistant handles setup and device management. Support for eight-node clusters in NVIDIA Sync is coming by the end of the year. 

Read on for benchmark data on how inference, orchestration, and training scale as the cluster grows.

...

## Run larger, newer frontier-class models

The biggest benefit of an eight-node cluster is memory. A single DGX Spark provides 128 GB of unified memory; four nodes reach 512 GB; eight nodes reach 1 TB. That capacity opens the door to a class of models that previously wouldn’t start on a four-node system, including the full GLM 5.3 (753B) model from Z.ai.

Beyond simply fitting these models, the cluster is designed to serve them interactively. As an early example, we ran GLM 5.3 Flash across an eight-node cluster, and measured roughly 80 tokens per second (TPS) in generation, suitable for interactive local development against a frontier-class mixture-of-experts model. 

The full GLM 5.3 (753B) checkpoint runs across the 8x 128 GB cluster, making it one of the largest open models you can serve locally.

| Concurrency | Prefill, total tokens per second (TPS) | Prefill, per user (TPS) | Decode, total (TPS) | Decode, per user (TPS) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 1,600 | 1,600 | 31 | 31

...

## Two, four, eight: Scaling the cluster

Low-latency NVIDIA ConnectX-7 NICs and RDMA on Converged Ethernet (RoCE) communication let DGX Spark nodes exchange tensors efficiently, so you can scale a model across more nodes to fit it in memory and to improve throughput. To isolate cluster scaling behavior and remove context-dependent behavior, we benchmarked a dense Qwen3.8-27B (NVFP4) model without speculative decoding/MTP across one to eight nodes:

signals.excerpt:
# Specter MoE System Reports 1.88x Peak Single-GPU Speedup 

 By Alexis Dufresne · Published October 21, 2026 at 08:09 UTC · Updated October 21, 2026 at 08:30 UTC 

## TL;DR

- Specter reports an average 1.50x speedup in time per output token, peaking at 1.88x, against the state-of-the-art MoE inference system on single-GPU hardware.
- A quantized draft model runs on the GPU while experts live in host memory; multi-step routing lookahead lets the runtime pre-stage expert transfers over PCIe.
- The authors have released code and the measured gains cover single-request inference only, not batched or multi-tenant serving.

Specter, a new MoE inference system, reports an average 1.50x speedup in time per output token with peaks hitting 1.88x over the state-of-the-art on commodity single-GPU hardware, according to its authors on Hugging Face. The paper targets a familiar bottleneck. Mixture-of-experts models often exceed a single accelerator's memory, so experts get pushed out to host memory, and the resulting PCIe traffic sits on the critical path because routing is data-dependent.

The method pairs quantization with speculative decoding. "Its lightweight quantized draft model runs efficiently on device while preserving high-fidelity expert activation patterns," the authors write, which gives the runtime "accurate multi-step lookahead over future expert usage" so expert movement can be organized ahead of verification rather than reactively.

Code is posted at the paper's GitHub repository. The reported speedups cover single-request inference; the abstract does not break out

signals.title: 15% More Accurate Than Unsloth: Qwen-3.8-27B Quants for Local Agents
signals.excerpt:
# 15% More Accurate Than Unsloth: Qwen-3.8-27B Quants for Local Agents 

Published October 22, 2026 

Prabod

Today we're releasing Qwen3.8-27B-BaseQuant-V1: quantised builds of Qwen3.8-27B in three sizes, each the same size as the matching Unsloth dynamic quant and each closer to the full-precision model. On prompts from six public datasets (coding agents, function calling and chat), BaseQuant has 15% lower KL divergence than Unsloth at both 3 and 4 bits, including UD-Q4_K_M, the size most people run.

| Size | BaseQuant | Same size as |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Small | `Qwen3.8-27B-BaseQuant-V1-Small.gguf` (10.93 GB) | Unsloth `UD-IQ3_XXS` (10.93 GB) |
| Medium | `Qwen3.8-27B-BaseQuant-V1-Medium.gguf` (16.41 GB) | Unsloth `UD-Q4_K_M` (16.46 GB) |
| Large | `Qwen3.8-27B-BaseQuant-V1-Large.gguf` (20.82 GB) | Unsloth `UD-Q5_K_XL` (20.88 GB) |

...

## Why agents need a closer quant 

An agent calls the model again and again: plan, call a tool, read the result, call the next one. Every step is conditioned on the steps before it, so a quant that drifts a little from the original at each step drifts a lot by the end of a task. A benchmark score hides this: two quants with the same accuracy can still disagree with the original on many individual answers.

So we measure what an agent actually depends on: how far the quantised model's next-token distribution is from the full-precision model's, at every position, as KL divergence. Lower means the quant behaves more like the model you meant to run.

...

### Public prompts 

Each number below is how much lower BaseQuant's KL divergence is than the Unsloth quant of the same size, so bigger is better.

| Public prompts |

...

## Try it 

With llama.cpp:

```sh
llama-server -hf basecompute/Qwen3.8-27B-BaseQuant-V1 -hff Qwen3.8-27B-BaseQuant-V1-Medium.gguf -c 32768 -ngl 99

```

With superfluid, which serves the OpenAI, Anthropic and Ollama APIs on top of it:

```sh
superfluid serve basecompute/Qwen3.8-27B-BaseQuant-V1 --runtime llamacpp --pull-file Qwen3.8-27B-BaseQuant-V1-Medium.gguf

```

The Medium and Large sizes also ship as `.base` bundles for the BaseRT engine.

...

## How we measured 

- Same size. Each BaseQuant file is no larger than the Unsloth quant it is compared with.
- Same engine. Both quants run in the same llama.cpp build against the same full-precision references.
- Per-token KL divergence from the full-precision model, averaged over every scored position. Intervals are bootstrapped over prompts.
- Held-out text was never used to build the models. The public prompt set is at basecompute/quant-fidelity-eval, with the selection script.

We're also releasing a 4-bit quant of Gemma 4 E4B-it, gemma-4-E4B-it-BaseQuant-V1, with results in the accompanying paper.

signals.title: Introducing vLLM TorchTPU | vLLM Blog
signals.excerpt:
# Introducing vLLM TorchTPU

October 20, 2026 6 min read

Table of Contents

Today we're releasing vLLM TorchTPU (`vllm-torchtpu`), a new backend for running vLLM on Google Cloud TPUs. It's built on Google's TorchTPU stack and runs the model definitions that already live in vLLM, so most models that work in vLLM today can be served on TPU without changes to the model code.

This work comes out of the engineering partnership between Inferact and Google we announced last month. Our goals for the project are to:

1. Make it easy to bring new models to TPU by reusing vLLM's existing model code.
2. Push TPU inference performance in open source, with Pallas kernels for attention, Mixture-of-Experts, and quantized matmul.
3. Keep the vLLM experience the same: the same CLI, OpenAI-compatible server, scheduler, and KV cache manager you use on other hardware.

...

### Models, Features, and What's Next

`vllm-torchtpu` can serve most models supported by vLLM, with TPU-specific kernel, quantization, and parallelism work for the Qwen, DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, Llama, GPT-OSS, and Gemma families. TPU v7x (Ironwood) is the recommended hardware and is tested in CI on every pull request; v6e, v5e, and v5p are experimental.

The Supported Models & Features page has the full list of validated checkpoints and features, with how to enable each one. The nightly support matrices track TPU v7x correctness and benchmark results from CI.

#### What's Next?

We want new open models from the major families (Qwen, DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi, Gemma, GPT-OSS) to run on TPU on the day they're released. Some of what's coming, from the public roadmap:

- An automated CI pipeline that onboards, benchmarks, and publishes support matrices for new open-weight models within 24 hours of release.
- Prefix-, cache-, and session-aware routing, and llm-d TPU memory-tier routing.
- PyTorch interfaces for Tokamax kernels, shared with other projects in the TorchTPU ecosystem.
- Diffusion model serving through `vllm-omni`.

Contributions are welcome!

# EAGLE-4 on AMD Instinct GPUs from day 0

 Oct 20, 2026

EAGLE-4, the newest drafter from the EAGLE team, runs on AMD Instinct™ MI355X GPUs from day 0, in SGLang and ATOM. - On Qwen3.8-27B, one MI355X GPU serves a single request at ~300 tokens/s in BF16: 3.5x plain decoding and 1.6x the model’s built-in MTP. - The gain holds as load grows, from 1 to 32 concurrent conversations, and scales to four GPUs. It works out of the box: the same checkpoint and the same serving flags as on other hardware.

## Day 0 on AMD Instinct GPUs

EAGLE-4 runs on the MI355X GPU with the same checkpoint and the same launch flags as elsewhere:

signals.excerpt:
MiniMax-M3.1 on AMD Instinct GPUs

# MiniMax-M3.1 on AMD Instinct GPUs: Day-0 support and optimization

 Oct 22, 2026

## TL;DR

- MiniMax-M3.1, MiniMax’s natively multimodal MoE model for coding and agent workloads (1M-token context, NVFP4 experts, a DSpark speculative-decoding draft), serves on AMD Instinct™ MI350 GPUs with both vLLM and ATOM on day 0.
- An MXFP4 checkpoint produced with AMD Quark, and an equivalent load-time conversion of the NVFP4 checkpoint, run the routed experts on AITER’s MXFP4 fused-MoE kernels; accuracy on both matches within the evaluation error on GSM8K, AIME and MMMU-Pro.
- vLLM: mono decode, one fused kernel launch per MoE layer for the whole decode step, cuts the per-token decode latency 3.2x at one request, 2.1x at four and 1.5x at sixteen compared with the same server with mono decode off, and gives 2.2-2.4x the interactivity on real coding-agent traces at 1-8 concurrent users.
- vLLM: DSpark speculative decoding composes with mono decode and adds about a third more interactivity at 1-4 users and 13% at 8; on its own it is the fallback where mono decode cannot run.
- ATOM: per-channel FP8 attention and a fused shared expert are applied at start-up, and the DSpark draft pass is CUDA-graph captured, accepting about half of its 7 drafts on real text.
- Serving commands for both engines and both checkpoints, for latency-bound (few users) and throughput-bound (many users) deployments, and for agentic workloads, are given in each engine’s section.

...

## Introduction

We are excited to announce Day-0 support for MiniMax-M3.1 on AMD Instinct™ MI350 Series GPUs across the AMD inference software stack: the ROCm™ build of vLLM and ATOM, the AMD inference engine, both running on ROCm with AITER kernels, with an MXFP4 checkpoint produced by AMD Quark. MiniMax-M3.1 is MiniMax’s latest natively multimodal Mixture-of-Experts model for coding and agent workloads, with a 1M-token context, built-in reasoning with selectable effort, native tool calling and a DSpark speculative-decoding draft.

...

## Day 0 support for AMD Instinct GPUs

MiniMax-M3.1 is supported on AMD Instinct MI350 Series GPUs in both inference engines from day 0: vLLM and ATOM. Both run the routed experts on AITER’s MXFP4 fused MoE with fp8 KV and index caches, AITER’s INT4 quick-reduce for the all-reduces, and tensor parallelism over 4 GPUs per model replica, so two replicas fit on an 8-GPU node. vLLM serves both checkpoints below (the MiniMax-M3.1-Flash release with its experts converted at load, and the Quark MXFP4 export); ATOM serves the Quark MXFP4 export. Where the two engines differ is in how they treat the MXFP8 attention linears and the shared expert at start-up, described in each engine’s section.

...

## Accuracy

Evaluated with lm-eval against the running server, per engine and checkpoint. GSM8K on the full 1,319-question test set (5-shot chat with the few-shot turns as prior chat turns, flexible / strict match); AIME 2025 and AIME 2026 as mean@16 (16 seeded passes, temperature 1.0, top_p 0.95); MMMU-Pro standard and vision splits (vision tower on). 0.791 / 0.682

- Wider mono steps. The 16-token step limit is why mono + DSpark stops at 4 concurrent requests and mono alone converges with mono-off at 32; wider steps are the next kernel item and the unlock for speculative decoding at 8-16 users.
- ATOM: mono decode for M3.1. Bring ATOM’s fused per-layer decode kernels, which serve MiniMax-M3’s small decode steps, to M3.1, including its DSpark verify steps; vLLM and SGLang with the ATOM plugin.

...

## Test configuration and disclaimer

vLLM results were measured on 4 GPUs of an 8x AMD Instinct MI350X node with ROCm 7.2, PyTorch 2.13, Triton 3.8, AITER 0.1.25 and FlyDSL 0.3.4, running a ROCm vLLM build with the MiniMax-M3.1 work described here, in October 2026. ATOM results were measured on 4 GPUs of an 8x AMD Instinct MI355X node in a ROCm ATOM development container with the MiniMax-M3.1 changes, in October 2026. Checkpoints: the MiniMax-M3.1 release and AMD’s Quark MXFP4 export of it. Serving-mode ratios come from vLLM’s serving benchmark with random prompts; agentic ratios from the InferenceX agentic-coding harness (AIPerf replay of recorded coding-agent traces) with one hour per point; accuracy from lm-eval. Results on other hardware, software versions, settings or workloads will differ; these figures are for illustration and are not a performance guarantee.

signals.excerpt:
Trending Open Source AI Projects on GitHub, October 2026 - DEV Community
Posted on Oct 21 • Originally published at glukhov.org
# Trending Open Source AI Projects on GitHub, October 2026
GitHub's monthly trending page works for a language, because a language filter already defines the set. Open source AI asks a different question: the work spans five languages, and the useful cut is the job a repository does.
This snapshot was read from the public GitHub API on 16 October 2026, and inside each group the repositories are ordered by star count. Stars measure attention, and a skills folder can gather that attention faster than a serving engine, so the group comes before the sort. The license column is part of the ranking as well, because several of the most starred projects are fair-code, brand-restricted, or split across two licenses.
The Rust and Go roundups on this site were built from that same page, with a language filter doing the grouping. Here the eight job groups below replace the filter, and each section states the trade that separates the close options. The closing sections turn the tables into a shortlist you can run, and into a repeatable method for the next snapshot.
### Search topics, then assign a job
GitHub topics are the workable substitute for a language filter. Sort a topic such as `ai-agents`, `llm`, `rag`, `local-llm`, or `agent-memory` by stars, and keep repositories that were pushed in the last few months. Free-text search for "AI" is too wide, and the unfiltered trending page still mixes agents with unrelated tools.
Three public inputs are enough to rebuild the list. Use topic search for the pool, a scenario catalog such as Top Open Source AI for the job labels, and the repository `LICENSE` file for the last column. That catalog publishes a composite of its own: stars at 70 percent, contributors at 10 percent, and update recency at 20 percent. This article keeps the simpler rule, so the number in the table is the number on GitHub.
Useful starting queries:
* ai-agents topic, by stars
* llm topic, by stars
* rag topic, by stars
* agent-memory topic above 5,000 stars
* GitHub trending, monthly
### Keep software, and set lists aside
A repository earns a row when someone can install it, or when it is a maintained harness that changes how an agent runs. Awesome-lists, prompt directories, and dumps of vendor system prompts collect stars and still leave nothing to deploy. They belong in a reading list, and they stay out of the tables below.
### Add a trending column only from your own snapshots
The language roundups could show stars gained in a month because GitHub already computes that delta inside one language. Across these groups, a monthly delta needs two snapshots of your own. Save `full\_name` and `stargazers\_count` on the first of the month, then subtract. Until that series exists, total stars are the honest ranking key. "Trending" in the title means actively maintained projects with the attention to match, as of this date.
```
flowchart TD
  topics[Topic search on GitHub]
  catalog[Scenario catalog]
  licenseFile[License file]
  drop[Set lists and prompt dumps aside]
  group[Assign each repo to one job]
  rank[Sort by stars inside the job]
  topics --> drop
  catalog --> group
  drop --> group
  group --> rank
  licenseFile --> rank
```
## Where the projects sit
These groups are layers you can stack. A coding assistant can call a gateway, a gateway can call Ollama or vLLM, and a memory service can sit beside either of them. Two products from the same layer are usually a second opinion, and they are rarely a better architecture.
```
flowchart TB
  agent[Personal agent]
  coder[Coding assistant]
  skills[Skills and harness]
  memory[Memory]
  docs[RAG and documents]
  flow[Workflow builder]
  gate[Model gateway]
  run[Local runtime]
  coder --> skills
  agent --> memory
  coder --> memory
  agent --> docs
  flow --> docs
  agent --> gate
  coder --> gate
  flow --> gate
  docs --> run
  gate --> run
```
## Personal AI assistants
This group is for agents that take actions on a machine or across tools, beyond a single coding session. OpenClaw leads by a wide margin. Hermes is the other general agent at this scale, and AutoGPT is the older name that is still accumulating stars while its license has split. A deeper leaderboard for this pair alone, with downloads, token share, and CVE history, is the OpenClaw vs Hermes Agent comparison.
|Project|Stars|License|Repository|
|OpenClaw|392,126|MIT|openclaw/openclaw|
|Hermes Agent|254,122|MIT|NousResearch/hermes-agent|
|Firecrawl|191,908|AGPL-3.0|firecrawl/firecrawl|
|AutoGPT|187,598|MIT and Polyform Shield|Significant-Gravitas/AutoGPT|
Firecrawl is listed here because agents need pages, and it is the web-data project readers actually star. It is a tool, and the assistants call it.
### OpenClaw
|Metric|Value|
|Repository|openclaw/openclaw|
|Stars|392,126|
|License|MIT|
|Language|TypeScript|
OpenClaw is a personal agent meant to run on your own operating system and carry out tasks, which is the plain reading of a project that calls itself an AI that does things on any platform. The star count is the largest in this article, and the MIT license is the permissive end of the set. Treat the install as a local automation runtime with broad access to the machine, and scope what it is allowed to touch before you leave it running.
### Hermes Agent
|Metric|Value|
|Repository|NousResearch/hermes-agent|
|Stars|254,122|
|License|MIT|
|Language|Python|
Hermes Agent, from Nous Research, is a general agent designed to accumulate skills and context as it is used. It sits in the same job as OpenClaw, with a Python codebase and the same MIT terms. Choose it when you want that growth loop and you are already comfortable operating a Python agent. Running both Hermes and OpenClaw means two permission models to audit.
### AutoGPT
|Metric|Value|
|Repository|Significant-Gravitas/AutoGPT|
|Stars|187,598|
|License|MIT outside autogpt\_platform; Polyform Shield inside it|
|Language|Python|
AutoGPT is the project that made autonomous agents a mainstream GitHub category, and it is still one of the most starred names in the set. The license is no longer a single grant. Everything outside the `autogpt\_platform` folder is MIT, and everything inside that folder is under the Polyform Shield License, which permits use but reserves the code's commercial value to the producer. Read that split before you build a product on the platform directory.
### Firecrawl
|Metric|Value|
|Repository|firecrawl/firecrawl|
|Stars|191,908|
|License|AGPL-3.0|
|Language|TypeScript|
Firecrawl turns sites into data that agents can call. The star count puts it among the assistants even though the job is acquisition, which says a lot about what people are wiring up in 2026. AGPL-3.0 matters if you modify it and offer the result as a service. For a personal agent that only calls a local or vendor endpoint, the license is a smaller constraint.
## AI coding assistants
Coding agents are the densest part of the 2026 list. OpenCode leads the fully open terminal and editor agents, with Codex and Gemini CLI close behind as the vendor CLIs that happen to be open source. OpenHands, Cline, and Goose are the other programs you can actually run.
Aider (49,567 stars, Apache-2.0), Continue (36,228, Apache-2.0), and Crush (28,669, FSL-1.1-MIT) are real coding tools in the next band. Crush's license is a Functional Source License that converts to MIT on the schedule written in the file. One coding agent is plenty. A second one is for a comparison week, and after that it is configuration you have to keep in sync.
|Project|Stars|License|Repository|
|OpenCode|213,922|MIT|anomalyco/opencode|
|Codex|129,395|Apache-2.0|openai/codex|
|Gemini CLI|107,389|Apache-2.0|google-gemini/gemini-cli|
|OpenHands|91,004|MIT|OpenHands/OpenHands|
|Cline|70,370|Apache-2.0|cline/cline|
|Goose|55,324|Apache-2.0|aaif-goose/goose|
### OpenCode
|Metric|Value|
|Repository|anomalyco/opencode|
|Stars|213,922|
|License|MIT|
|Language|TypeScript|
OpenCode is an open source coding agent with a terminal workflow and a large plugin surface. It has become the default name people cite when they want a coding agent they can inspect, and the MIT license matches that use. The repository is anomalyco/opencode. Pick it when the agent itself should be something you can patch.
### Codex
|Metric|Value|
|Repository|openai/codex|
|Stars|129,395|
|License|Apache-2.0|
|Language|Rust|
Codex is OpenAI's lightweight coding agent for the terminal, written in Rust and licensed Apache-2.0. It is the open client for a hosted model family, which is a different bargain from a local-first agent. Use it when your team already standardizes on OpenAI models and you want a CLI you can automate. The client being open does not move the model weights onto your disk.
### Gemini CLI
|Metric|Value|
|Repository|google-gemini/gemini-cli|
|Stars|107,389|
|License|Apache-2.0|
|Language|TypeScript|
Gemini CLI brings Gemini into the terminal as an agent, under Apache-2.0. It plays the same role as Codex for a different provider, and the TypeScript codebase is easier to embed in existing Node tooling. Choose it when Gemini is the model you already pay for. Running it beside Codex is reasonable only if each repo has one default agent.
### OpenHands
|Metric|Value|
|Repository|OpenHands/OpenHands|
|Stars|91,004|
|License|MIT|
|Language|TypeScript|
OpenHands is a software-development agent with a full task loop, now published from the `OpenHands` organization. The MIT license and the higher-level product make it a platform choice, closer to a hosted development environment you can self-host than to a single binary. Use it when you want issues, sandboxes, and a UI around the agent. For a one-person terminal workflow, OpenCode, Codex, or Goose is the smaller install.
### Cline
|Metric|Value|
|Repository|cline/cline|
|Stars|70,370|
|License|Apache-2.0|
|Language|TypeScript|
Cline is an autonomous coding agent that ships as an SDK, an IDE extension, or a CLI. Apache-2.0 and the editor integration make it the practical pick for people who live in VS Code and still want a library they can call. It overlaps OpenCode more than it overlaps a chat UI. Standardize on one of them per repository so reviews stay readable.
### Goose
|Metric|Value|
|Repository|aaif-goose/goose|
|Stars|55,324|
|License|Apache-2.0|
|Language|Rust|
Goose is an extensible local agent that installs, edits, runs, and tests code with whatever model you point at it. The repository now lives at `aaif-goose/goose`, and the Rust implementation plus Apache-2.0 make it a strong workstation agent. Choose Goose when the model provider should be swappable and the agent should run on the machine that holds the code. It is a quieter star count than OpenCode, and it is a more direct fit for a local model.
## Agent skills and harnesses
Topic search will put this group above several real products. Superpowers and ECC are instructions, hooks, and workflows for agents you already run. Spec Kit is GitHub's own process toolkit for spec-driven development. They change agent behavior, and they are still software you compose with a coding assistant from the previous section.
|Project|Stars|License|Repository|
|Superpowers|299,886|MIT|obra/superpowers|
|ECC|280,382|MIT|affaan-m/ECC|
|Spec Kit|141,439|MIT|github/spec-kit|
### Superpowers
|Metric|Value|
|Repository|obra/superpowers|
|Stars|299,886|
|License|MIT|
|Language|Shell|
Superpowers is an agentic skills framework and a software-development methodology, distributed mostly as shell and instruction files under MIT. The star count is what you get when a method spreads through coding-agent users in a few months. Install it on top of an agent you already trust, and expect to edit the skills to match the repository. The framework will follow whatever permissions that agent already has.
### ECC
|Metric|Value|
|Repository|affaan-m/ECC|
|Stars|280,382|
|License|MIT|
|Language|JavaScript|
ECC is a harness for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, and similar agents, covering skills, memory, and checks around how the agent works. It is the right shape if you want the same loop on more than one coding agent. It is also another moving layer between you and the model. Adopt it when the team has already picked the agents and wants one shared way to brief them.
### Spec Kit
|Metric|Value|
|Repository|github/spec-kit|
|Stars|141,439|
|License|MIT|
|Language|Python|
Spec Kit is GitHub's toolkit for spec-driven development and the process around it. The maintainer is the platform most of these repositories already live on, and the MIT license is straightforward. Use it when you want a written spec before the agent edits code. It will stay quiet if the team treats the spec as optional paperwork.
## AI memory
Memory is the layer that lets an agent resume. The starred projects split into two styles. claude-mem, Beads, and much of Hindsight attach memory to coding sessions. Mem0, Cognee, and Letta are services you call from application agents. Capture policy, dependencies, and self-hosting tradeoffs for these backends are compared in Agent Memory Providers.
Memvid (16,600 stars, Apache-2.0) and Zep (4,961 stars, Apache-2.0) are smaller options in the same job, Memvid as a single-file store and Zep as an integration-heavy memory API. One memory system per agent is the setup you can still explain later.
|Project|Stars|License|Repository|
|claude-mem|101,052|Apache-2.0|thedotmack/claude-mem|
|Mem0|67,243|Apache-2.0|mem0ai/mem0|
|Hindsight|50,055|MIT|vectorize-io/hindsight|
|Cognee|32,364|Apache-2.0|topoteretes/cognee|
|Beads|27,917|MIT|gastownhall/beads|
|Letta|25,156|Apache-2.0|letta-ai/letta|
### claude-mem
|Metric|Value|
|Repository|thedotmack/claude-mem|
|Stars|101,052|
|License|Apache-2.0|
|Language|TypeScript|
claude-mem records what a coding agent does, compresses that history, and injects the relevant part into later sessions. It talks to Claude Code, OpenClaw, Codex, Gemini CLI, Hermes, Copilot, and OpenCode, which is why it leads this group. Apache-2.0 fits a sidecar you may want to modify. Use it when the thing you keep forgetting is the coding session itself.
### Mem0
|Metric|Value|
|Repository|mem0ai/mem0|
|Stars|67,243|
|License|Apache-2.0|
|Language|Python|
Mem0 is a memory layer for agents and applications, with user, session, and agent state behind an API. It is the default name when the product is a support bot or a personal assistant, and you want that memory outside any one coding tool. Apache-2.0 and a hosted option sit side by side, so self-hosting is a choice you can make later. Prefer it over a coding-session hook when many agents should share the same facts about a user.
### Hindsight
|Metric|Value|
|Repository|vectorize-io/hindsight|
|Stars|50,055|
|License|MIT|
|Language|Python|
Hindsight is Vectorize's agent memory project, aimed at agents that learn from what they have already done, and it integrates with both coding agents and application frameworks. The MIT license is the most permissive in this group. The project publishes strong benchmark claims, and those claims should be re-run on your own transcripts before you bet a product on them. Pick Hindsight when you want a dedicated memory service and you are willing to compare it with Mem0 on your data.
### Cognee
|Metric|Value|
|Repository|topoteretes/cognee|
|Stars|32,364|
|License|Apache-2.0|
|Language|Python|
Cognee builds a memory and knowledge graph that agents can query, with an emphasis on running that layer on smaller models. It overlaps Mem0 and it also overlaps the RAG tools below, because a graph of your documents behaves like both memory and retrieval. Apache-2.0 keeps the embedding path replaceable. Choose it when the facts you care about are entities and relationships, and a flat vector index has already felt too lossy.
### Beads
|Metric|Value|
|Repository|gastownhall/beads|
|Stars|27,917|
|License|MIT|
|Language|Go|
Beads stores coding-agent tasks, plans, and dependencies as files that travel with the git branch. The repository is now `gastownhall/beads`, and it is the same project the January Go roundup listed under its earlier path. MIT and a git-backed store make it the memory tool that your existing review process can see. Use it when context should fork with the branch. Use claude-mem or Mem0 when the memory has to outlive a single repository.
### Letta
|Metric|Value|
|Repository|letta-ai/letta|
|Stars|25,156|
|License|Apache-2.0|
|Language|Python|
Letta is the stateful-agent platform that grew out of MemGPT. Memory here is part of the agent runtime, so the agent manages its own context as a feature of the platform. That is a deeper commitment than dropping Mem0 under an agent you already run. Apache-2.0 applies to the open platform. Choose Letta when you want the runtime and the memory designed together, and choose Mem0 when you want memory under agents you do not intend to replace.
## RAG and knowledge bases
RAG projects turn documents into a context layer. RAGFlow is the end-to-end engine people are starring. LlamaIndex is the document framework, GraphRAG is Microsoft's graph approach, and WeKnora is Tencent's knowledge platform, which also appeared in the January Go roundup and has kept growing.
|Project|Stars|License|Repository|
|RAGFlow|92,289|Apache-2.0|infiniflow/ragflow|
|LlamaIndex|52,513|MIT|run-llama/llama\_index|
|GraphRAG|36,349|MIT|microsoft/graphrag|
|WeKnora|34,210|MIT|Tencent/WeKnora|
### RAGFlow
|Metric|Value|
|Repository|infiniflow/ragflow|
|Stars|92,289|
|License|Apache-2.0|
|Language|Go|
RAGFlow is a self-hosted RAG engine that parses messy documents and exposes retrieval to agents, with citations as part of the product. Apache-2.0 and a UI you can hand to a team are why it leads this group by a clear gap. Use it when the job is "put our files behind an answer box" and you want the parser, the index, and the API from one project. Reach for LlamaIndex when you are embedding retrieval inside an application you already control.
### LlamaIndex
|Metric|Value|
|Repository|run-llama/llama\_index|
|Stars|52,513|
|License|MIT|
|Language|Python|
LlamaIndex is a document-processing framework for agents and RAG pipelines. It is a library with many connectors, and the MIT license fits that role. You assemble the index, the store, and the agent yourself, which is the cost of the flexibility. Choose it for product code. Choose RAGFlow when you want the same job as a service you deploy.
### GraphRAG
|Metric|Value|
|Repository|microsoft/graphrag|
|Stars|36,349|
|License|MIT|
|Language|Python|
GraphRAG builds a graph over a corpus and answers questions by walking that graph, as Microsoft Research's open implementation of the idea. The technique itself is explained in Advanced RAG: LongRAG, Self-RAG and GraphRAG. MIT licensing makes it easy to try beside a vector pipeline. Graph construction costs more up front than a chunk-and-embed index, and it pays that cost back on questions that span many documents. Use it when the corpus has structure you are currently forcing into chunks.
### WeKnora
|Metric|Value|
|Repository|Tencent/WeKnora|
|Stars|34,210|
|License|MIT|
|Language|Go|
WeKnora is Tencent's knowledge platform for turning documents into a RAG index, an agent, and a wiki that the project describes as self-maintaining. The project license is MIT, with third-party components under their own terms. GitHub reports that license as Other, because the MIT grant sits under a Tencent preamble. It is the closest cousin to RAGFlow in this table, with a Go core. Prefer it when you want the wiki and the agent in the same box, and compare the parsers on a sample of your own PDFs before you migrate a library.
## Workflow and agent builders
Builders are where a team draws the flow, or where a developer imports the framework that draws it for them. n8n is the largest by stars and the narrowest by license. Dify and Langflow are the AI-native studios. LangChain is the library underneath a great many of the others.
CrewAI (59,745 stars, MIT) and AutoGen (61,429 stars, CC-BY-4.0) belong in the same conversation as code-first multi-agent frameworks. AutoGen's Creative Commons attribution license is unusual for a code repository, and it is worth reading before you vendor it. LangChain remains the integration surface those frameworks still meet.
|Project|Stars|License|Repository|
|n8n|207,535|Sustainable Use License|n8n-io/n8n|
|Dify|158,591|Modified Apache-2.0|langgenius/dify|
|Langflow|155,717|MIT|langflow-ai/langflow|
|LangChain|147,886|MIT|langchain-ai/langchain|
### n8n
|Metric|Value|
|Repository|n8n-io/n8n|
|Stars|207,535|
|License|Sustainable Use License|
|Language|TypeScript|
n8n is a workflow platform with hundreds of integrations and native AI steps, and it is the project people mean when they want Zapier-style automation they can host. The Sustainable Use License allows internal business use, personal use, and non-commercial use. Distribution is limited to free, non-commercial copies, and files marked `.ee` need a separate enterprise license. It is source-available fair-code, and it is still the right tool for internal automation if those limits match how you run it.
### Dify
|Metric|Value|
|Repository|langgenius/dify|
|Stars|158,591|
|License|Modified Apache-2.0|
|Language|TypeScript|
Dify is a workspace for agent workflows and RAG pipelines, with model providers and tools in one deployable stack. The license starts from Apache-2.0 and adds conditions: operating a multi-tenant service, meaning multiple workspaces, needs a commercial license, and the console logo and copyright notice stay on the frontend. Single-tenant internal use is the case the extra clauses leave open. Choose Dify when a team needs one UI from prototype to production, and choose Langflow when the license has to stay plain MIT.
### Langflow
|Metric|Value|
|Repository|langflow-ai/langflow|
|Stars|155,717|
|License|MIT|
|Language|Python|
Langflow is a visual builder for agents and RAG flows, with an MIT license and a star count essentially tied with Dify. The canvas is the product, and the generated flows are something a developer can still own. Use it when you want a diagram of the pipeline and a license a procurement checklist already understands. The trade is a younger application surface than Dify's workspace features.
### LangChain
|Metric|Value|
|Repository|langchain-ai/langchain|
|Stars|147,886|
|License|MIT|
|Language|Python|
LangChain is the agent-engineering library that most integration docs still assume. MIT and the breadth of connectors keep it in every shortlist, and the abstraction cost is real once the chain is doing something simple. Use it when you are writing application code and you want the adapters already written. Use Dify or Langflow when the deliverable is a workspace, and use a direct provider SDK when the flow is a handful of calls.

AWS Neuron 2.33 adds native PyTorch support, Neuron Observer, and other new features - AWS

# AWS Neuron 2.33 adds native PyTorch support, Neuron Observer, and other new features

 Posted on: Oct 21, 2026 

AWS Neuron 2.33 is now available, introducing TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium, in public beta. You can run models written with the standard PyTorch APIs on Amazon EC2 Trn2 and Trn3 instances, in eager mode or with torch.compile. This release also introduces Neuron Observer in public beta, which detects Trainium health issues in under a second and identifies the affected node or device.

The vLLM Neuron plugin upgrades to vLLM 0.29.0, and the vLLM Omni Neuron plugin for Wan2.2 video generation is now part of the Neuron release. Both support native PyTorch compilation through TorchNeuron. A new Neuron Deep Learning AMI and Deep Learning Container for PyTorch training include TorchNeuron, PyTorch 2.14, and TorchTitan. Neuron Explorer opens profiles captured with torch.profiler. From a PyTorch memory snapshot, it now attributes allocations to the Python source lines that made them, for debugging out-of-memory errors in eager mode.

Kernels written with the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) can now use the full Python language for metaprogramming, including generators and class inheritance. The NKI Library adds 25 new experimental kernels, including kernels for DeepSeek-V3.2, Qwen3.5, and Kimi Delta Attention.

signals.title: Day-0 Support for Flint on vLLM | vLLM Blog
signals.excerpt:
# Day-0 Support for Flint on vLLM

October 21, 2026 5 min read

Table of Contents

vLLM supports Recursive's Flint from day 0. Both its NVFP4 and BF16 checkpoints run on a single GPU, and a single request decodes at about 500 tokens/s on one GB200, even with 100K tokens of context.

Flint is a 40B-parameter MoE that activates only about 2.5B parameters per token, with sliding-window attention in most layers and a 262K-token context. It ships as two separate checkpoints: NVFP4 (quantization-aware trained) and BF16.

...

Flint support is being merged into vLLM (#62938). With a vLLM build that includes it, serve the same way:

Copy code

```
# NVFP4 checkpoint (GGUF): config and tokenizer come from the BF16 repo
vllm serve RecursiveSI/flint-nvfp4-gguf \
  --hf-config-path RecursiveSI/flint --tokenizer RecursiveSI/flint \
  --enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser glm47 \
  --reasoning-parser glm47 --exclude-tools-when-tool-choice-none
 
# BF16 checkpoint
vllm serve RecursiveSI/flint \
  --enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser glm47 \
  --reasoning-parser glm47 --exclude-tools-when-tool-choice-none
```

...

The NVFP4 checkpoint is a GGUF file whose blocks are NVIDIA's NVFP4 format in a different byte order. vLLM repacks it losslessly at load time and runs it weight-only (W4A16), with BF16 activations and KV cache, as Recursive's reference implementation does. Every Flint kernel follows the reference's rounding points, and accuracy matches it on GSM8K, GPQA-Diamond, long-context MRCR and a tool-calling suite.

...

In total, NVFP4 decode went from 4.81 to 1.78 ms (2.7×), BF16 decode from 3.53 to 2.34 ms (1.5×), and an 8K-token prefill from 207 to 145 ms (1.4×). A forward now runs 346 kernels instead of 1,096. Served end to end, batch-1 decode at 100K context takes 2.06 ms per token (about 485 tokens/s), which is the forward plus the LM head and sampling.

signals.excerpt:
AI Runtime is Generally Available | Databricks Blog

October 21, 2026

# AI Runtime is Generally Available

Train foundation models faster on your enterprise data with fully managed GPU infrastructure

by Tejas Sundaresan, Jianwei Xie, Mike Del Balso, Hanlin Tang, Julia Powell and Cynthya Peranandam 

Summary

- AI Runtime is now generally available, bringing high-performance GPU infrastructure directly into Databricks.
- Scale reliably and experiment faster with seconds-level launches, flexible environments, and integrated observability — without the overhead of managing GPU infrastructure.
- Keep every training workload secure and governed with built-in Unity Catalog controls and workload isolation — in a new era of agent-led training.

Today, we’re excited to announce the General Availability of AI Runtime (AIR), bringing fully managed GPU infrastructure directly into Databricks so customers can train their most demanding models where their enterprise data already lives.

Too often, AI teams spend more time securing GPU capacity, managing failures, and waiting for experiments to launch than improving their models. Running GPU infrastructure separately from their Lakehouse adds governance gaps and puts sensitive training data at risk. As coding agents drive more training experiments, these bottlenecks and risks grow — making reliable, fast, and governed infrastructure essential.

AIR brings GPU infrastructure, developer tools, and data governance together so teams can train at scale, iterate faster, and secure every workload without managing a separate GPU stack. Hundreds of companies, including Tubi, Robinhood, PicPay, Merck, Flo Health, TinyFish, and FactSet, already use AIR to train and ship deep learning models to production, with use cases spanning healthcare, manufacturing, and consumer-facing agents. Our own Databricks AI Research team uses AIR to train the models behind KARL and AI Parse.

With AIR, customers can:

- Train at scale with hassle-free GPU infrastructure: Serverless, on-demand access to advanced GPUs backed by reliable multinode training, optimized performance, and battle-tested by 100,000+ GPU-hour training runs.
- Experiment faster with near-instant launch latency and easy debugging: Bring your own code, containers, and Ray workloads – and obtain seconds-level launch latency on RDMA-enabled GPUs. Environment caching and built-in debugging tools to save time on every training loop.
- Secure and govern every GPU workload: AIR operates within the governance perimeter of Databricks and Unity Catalog, and is backed by years of investment in Serverless security. AIR helps ensure GPU workloads protect valuable training data, comply with access policies, and are tracked/auditable.
